On each price bar, green is a deal, amber is thin and red is a pass; the black mark is the book's current price.

Trend picks

Trend picks come from the situation rather than the model: record, scoring margin, recent form, home/road splits, rest, overtime the night before, streaks and bad losses. Each factor shows how often teams in that spot won in past games; factors that never held up are listed but not counted. A side needs at least 3 live factors and a clear edge over the opponent's. The ladder compares every way to bet the side against the model's fair price, and the grade says whether the price leaves anything on the table. Trends are often already in the price, so many trend picks grade C or D. They're tracked as their own category so the record shows whether they beat the model.

No side has enough situational factors (at least 3 that have held up historically) on this slate.

Who's missing

College programs don't publish injury reports, so this lists rotation players (15+ minutes a game) who missed their team's most recent game or games. The model treats a player who missed the last game as 55% to play, two straight as 25%, three or more as 12%. Value is what he is worth per game over a replacement player, in points of margin. How it works

Data. Box scores for this season and last come from ESPN via the sportsdataverse data releases on GitHub, topped up with ESPN game summaries for anything newer. The schedule, sportsbook lines (ESPN's odds feed, usually DraftKings), AP rankings and rosters come from ESPN's public API. Every Division I game is modelled; non-Division I opponents share one rating.

Team ratings. Each team gets an offensive, defensive and tempo rating per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent and home court (neutral sites count as neutral), from a weighted regression where a game 45 days ago counts half as much as last night. The preseason rating starts from last season: the team's level relative to its conference keeps 60%, the conference's level is kept in full, and roster moves are added on top. Returning players, transfers in and players lost are valued by their game score per 40 minutes; freshmen and newcomers without Division I history count as a little above replacement. That preseason rating is worth about 5 games, so by mid-December this season's results dominate.

Who's missing. College programs don't publish injury reports. A rotation player (15+ minutes) who missed the team's last game is treated as 55% to play, two straight as 25%, three or more as 12%. In the 2025-26 test this helped only a little, so the adjustment is kept light. Check team news before betting.

Game estimate. Tempo times efficiency gives each team's points. For betting, the model is blended with the market when a line is posted: 35% model on the spread and moneyline, 25% on totals. Results land within about 11 points of the spread estimate and 16.9 of the total estimate (one standard deviation), which sets every probability. First-half lines use the same estimate scaled to the half.

How good is it? Re-run day by day through 2025-26 with no hindsight and checked against 1,454 real DraftKings closing lines, the model alone missed the final margin by 11.3 points (root mean square) against 11.0 for the closing spread, and blends with some model weight beat the line alone. The pick rule used here (35% model on sides, a 2-point safety margin, nothing where the model is 6+ points off the spread) went 127-102 on spreads (55.5%, +7.3% per bet) and returned +4.2% on moneylines at closing prices. On totals the line was better than the model (17.0 vs 17.2 points), so totals need a much bigger edge and rarely make the list. Those settings were chosen on the same games, so expect real results to be thinner. Disagreements of 6+ points went 19-25 for the model, which usually means the market knew something: those are listed as warnings, not bets.

Players. Minutes come from recent games for the current team (coach's-decision DNPs count as zero), blended with last season, then spread to 200 per team, capped at 38. Per-minute rates weight recent games most and are scaled so the team's players add up to its projected points, with tempo and the opponent's rebounds and assists allowed. Each stat's spread comes from the player's own game log, widened for uncertainty.

Odds. Fair is the break-even price for our probability. Bet at subtracts a safety margin (2.0 points for sides, 3.5 for game totals, 3.5 for team totals and halves, 4.5 for props). At Bet at or better is value, between Bet at and Fair is a lean, worse than Fair is a pass.

Top bets. Only markets with a real sportsbook price qualify. A pick is either high probability (our 58%+) or value, and every pick must beat the Bet-at price (the rule tested above). The list alternates between the two, takes at most 2 per game and never both sides of one market, and skips sides where the model alone is 6+ points off the spread or totals 9+ off.

Limits. Suspensions, illnesses and players sitting aren't known until they miss a game. Lines move a lot on small college games; get the best number you can. I'm not a financial advisor; bet only what you can afford to lose.

Grades, trends and units

Grades. Every pick gets a score out of 100: edge at the price (30), win chance (10), how close the model is to the market (10; a huge gap usually means news the model can't see), whether situational trends back the side (30) and how much the model's claimed edge has held up in that bet type (20). A is 68+, B 56+, C 44+, D below. Unpriced picks and early-season picks top out at B. Hover a grade for the breakdown.

Trend picks. Each side is checked for situational factors: a better record, scoring margin or recent form, a home/road split, the opponent on a back-to-back or coming off overtime, rest, streaks and the opponent's last loss being to a worse team. Each factor's record comes from past games, and only factors that won more than half the time (after mixing in 60 games of 50/50) count. A trend pick needs 3+ of them and a net edge over the opponent's factors. The "ways to bet it" ladder compares the moneyline, regulation or spread and team total against the model's fair price, and the play is the one with the best expected return.

Suggested units. 0.25 Kelly (1 unit = 1% of a bankroll), rounded to half units and capped at 3u. Before sizing, the model's win chance is pulled toward the market by the bet type's trust: trust = the share of the model's claimed edge that has actually shown up in graded results, starting at 50% and updating as games finish. A bet type that has matched the market and not the model gets small or zero units.

Scatter. On the Track record tab every priced pick is placed by its edge at the price (across) and the price (up), coloured by result, with upcoming picks as rings. Zones shade areas where at least 5 graded picks made or lost money, so you can see whether tonight's picks sit where past ones paid.
